overview: “Caribbean hunter-gatherers” is the atlas’s map label, not one people. From 1500 BCE to 700 CE its polygon bundles parts of Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles, Barbados, Venezuela and the Guianas. Then it shrinks, splits, disappears from most islands, returns in 1500, and ends as a tiny mainland patch in 1700. Those jumps reflect changing atlas categories, Ciboney, Arawaks, Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and colonial states, not synchronized migrations or extinctions. Real Caribbean communities had different histories. Some fished, gathered shellfish, hunted, gardened and used pottery in changing combinations; none stayed frozen as “hunter-gatherers” for 3,200 years. Canoes connected islands, while ornaments, stone, food and stories traveled through overlapping networks. Archaeologists recover postholes, hearths, burials, food residues, teeth, bones, ancient DNA and even coprolites. Yes, ancient poo can become scientific treasure: it preserves plant fragments, parasites and microbes. Homes could be rebuilt quickly after hurricanes, children learned skilled work by watching and practicing, and families cared for babies with locally specific feeding traditions. European invasion brought warfare, enslavement, epidemic disease, forced labor and displacement, yet Indigenous people resisted and survived. Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and other descendant communities remain living peoples. The map’s 1700 deletion is not their ending.

periods.title: Many early island and coastal communities beneath one fixed polygon
periods.summary: The atlas repeats one twenty-five-part shape across three intervals. Archaeology instead finds locally dated settlements, different stone traditions, fishing and gathering, plant cultivation and some early pottery. Direct radiocarbon dating at Barbados and Montserrat matters because artifact labels alone cannot make every island follow the same sequence.

periods.title: Ceramic traditions, older communities and growing networks overlap
periods.summary: Eleven exact atlas intervals keep the old geometry unchanged. Across the region, Saladoid, Huecoid and other archaeological traditions describe pottery and practice, not guaranteed ethnic groups. Movements from northern South America, continuing earlier island communities and new exchange networks produced mosaics rather than a single replacement event.

periods.title: Connected island societies before the atlas’s first great contraction
periods.summary: Three more intervals preserve the original shape through 700 to 800. Farming, fishing, craft and travel varied by island, and genetic evidence finds both long continuities and new ancestry without equating ancestry with language. At 800 the map suddenly removes most components, an editorial seam rather than a dated regional collapse.

periods.title: The umbrella loses Greater and Lesser Antillean territory
periods.summary: The target retains Puerto Rico, Barbados, Paria and one additional component, while tested Cuban and Hispaniolan points become “Ciboney” and Lesser Antillean points “Arawaks.” Those are other atlas labels, not proof that one homogeneous population was pushed aside on a single date.

periods.title: Named atlas neighbors expand while only three components remain
periods.summary: Across five exact intervals, tested Greater Antillean points belong to “Taíno,” several Lesser Antillean points to “Arawaks,” and this id retains Barbados and Paria. Archaeological exchange crossed those digital lines; pottery styles, household forms and political organization still varied through time and place.

periods.title: A duplicate target layer beside Taíno and Kalinago labels
periods.summary: The 1400 file contains two separate target polygons: one around Paria and another near the Amazon mouth. Tested islands belong to Taíno or Kalinago layers. This unusual split confirms that the label is a cartographic catchall; it cannot stand in for every community Europeans later encountered.

periods.title: Invasion begins while the atlas keeps only one mainland patch
periods.summary: In the 1492 snapshot, named Indigenous layers cover the tested islands and this id survives only near the Amazon mouth. Spanish invasion began war, raiding, forced labor and settlement; Indigenous diplomacy and resistance also began immediately. The map seam is not a population count.

periods.title: A cartographic return amid accelerating colonial violence
periods.summary: The atlas restores three components, again including Barbados and Paria, just eight years after removing them. That reversal is an editorial inconsistency. In lived history, raids, encomienda, disease and coerced food production fractured communities while people fled, negotiated, fought and maintained households.

periods.title: Residual mainland polygons and persistent Indigenous networks
periods.summary: Two mainland components remain as European colonial labels take many island points. Kalinago and other Indigenous networks continued movement, exchange and alliance across the Windwards and Guianas; European goods entered existing systems rather than erasing local choices. Colonial categories often served enslavement and war.

periods.title: The final tiny component is a map endpoint, not extinction
periods.summary: Only an Amazon-mouth polygon remains through 1700, when the exact id disappears. Colonial expansion, Indigenous resistance, African maroon communities and new alliances continued beyond that date. Living Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and other descendants make any “vanished people” ending historically false.

items.text: The live index calls this a culture, dates it approximately from 1500 BCE to 1700 and supplies no historical summary. Coverage finds thirty consecutive intervals and thirty border files but no card. The exact id is preserved for software compatibility; the label itself needs a warning.

From 1500 BCE through 700 CE, the same MultiPolygon has 25 parts, 596 coordinate positions and bounds reaching from roughly 84.71°W to 48.40°W and 1.74°S to 23.14°N. A perfectly frozen border for 2,200 years signals editorial geometry, not surveyed territory.

At 800 the shape drops to four parts and at 1000 to three. Tested island points change to Ciboney, Arawaks and Taíno owners, while Barbados and Paria remain here. These are layer-to-layer classification changes; the coordinates do not document an invasion, language frontier or mass departure.

The 1400 file contains two exact features with the same id: a 92-position Paria polygon and a separate 25-position Amazon-mouth polygon. In 1492 only the smaller one remains; in 1500 three components return. That duplicate-and-return sequence is an atlas oddity, not a recoverable ancient border.

By 1530, tested islands and Paria carry colonial or named Indigenous layers while this id retreats to untested mainland remnants. At 1650 only one small polygon remains; at 1700 it vanishes. No evidence supports treating that deletion as a people’s conquest, migration or extinction.

sections.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories

items.text: Caribbean archaeology combines stratigraphy, artifacts, plant and animal remains, burials, settlement plans and direct dates. Its basic achievement is regional comparison without assuming islands were isolated. Canoe travel connected them to one another and to surrounding mainlands for millennia before European arrival.

At eight Cuban sites, researchers measured carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and strontium isotopes in 146 people. Results show varied diets and movement among communities often lumped into an “Archaic” label. Isotopes describe sampled lives and childhood geology; they do not reveal a person’s language or self-name.

A 2026 preprint reports early genome-wide data from four people on Hispaniola’s Samaná Peninsula and compares them with Cuba and later Caribbean samples. It suggests long pre-Ceramic continuity plus local structure, but remains unreviewed and sparsely sampled. Genetics cannot turn an atlas polygon into one population.

A larger ancient-DNA study analyzes 174 people, detects multiple movements and even relatives buried on different islands. Such work can illuminate ancestry and mobility, never culture by itself. Researchers must also respect descendant communities, destructive sampling limits and the uneven survival of tropical human remains.

Colonial writers called very different people “Carib,” often to mark enemies or justify enslavement. Ancient DNA from the Lesser Antilles shows why modern researchers must test, rather than inherit, those labels. Pottery style, ancestry, political alliance and spoken language are separate questions with different evidence.

sections.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors

items.text: The first island voyagers crossed water beyond sight of land, and later communities maintained routes through currents, winds and seasonal seas. Boats rarely survive, so archaeologists infer travel from island settlement, transported stone, animals, plants and human movement. “Island” never meant “alone.”

Montserrat’s early deposits and Antigua’s valuable chert sources help date movement through the eastern Caribbean. Direct radiocarbon results can overturn old migration diagrams, while stone sourcing traces journeys. A tool’s rock may tell where material began, though not who paddled it or why.

Hurricanes, storm surges, drought and scarce freshwater repeatedly challenged settlements. Archaeology suggests flexible food systems and houses built from local materials could favor quick recovery. That was skilled resilience, not proof that storms were harmless; different islands and households faced unequal risks.

Human communities altered island ecologies by moving plants and animals, clearing or burning land and harvesting coasts, but impacts varied. Some fish or shellfish records show sustained use over centuries; others indicate pressure. “People damaged nature” and “people lived perfectly sustainably” are both too simple.

Hutia bones are not just leftover dinner. Isotope work in the Dominican Republic compares rodent diets across habitats and asks whether animals fed within human-made niches. The result reveals changing proximity between people, gardens and endemic animals without assuming every hutia was domesticated or eaten.

sections.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared

items.text: No single “hunter-gatherer menu” fits this layer. Fish, shellfish, crabs, birds, rodents, fruits, roots, maize, beans, peppers and other plants appear in different combinations. Gardens and wild foods could coexist, so archaeologists increasingly describe mixed food systems instead of forcing every site into farmer-versus-forager boxes.

DNA and starch from Puerto Rican coprolites identify maize, sweet potato, chili, peanut, papaya, tomato and other plants, yet absence is not proof a food was never eaten. Cooking, digestion, season and tropical decay destroy traces. Ancient poo is gross-looking scientific gold, but it is still a tiny sample.

Cassava needs careful language. Toxic varieties require grating, squeezing and cooking, but starch studies also find sweet potato, maize and beans, sometimes where cassava was expected. Flat ceramic griddles are clues, not automatic “cassava labels”; residue, tool use-wear and context must agree.

Organic molecules absorbed into Isla de Mona pottery show plant processing during early colonial occupation. Historical and archaeological evidence indicates cassava bread production intensified for Spanish supply under coercive labor. A familiar Indigenous food thus became entangled with an imposed export economy, without losing local knowledge.

Dental calculus, the hardened plaque nobody wants at the dentist, can trap plant particles, proteins and microbial DNA. Puerto Rican samples reveal diet and oral ecology, but contamination and preservation require strict controls. One mouth records one life; it cannot supply a menu for every island.

sections.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements

items.text: Stone flakes, ground tools, shell implements, fiber, wood and pottery supported fishing, gardening, cooking and repair. Labels such as Lithic, Archaic, Saladoid or Ostionoid organize changing assemblages; they are research tools, not passports carried by one fixed people from island to island.

Lesser Antillean exchange operated at several scales. Everyday stone and pottery, visible ornaments and rare ceremonial valuables moved in different rhythms. Sourcing raw materials and studying manufacture let archaeologists rebuild relationships; an imported bead signals a connection, not necessarily a merchant, tribute or migration.

Before 1492, polished wood, greenstone, shell, guanín metal and food already circulated in systems of value. European beads and bells initially entered those networks, then became entangled with tribute and extraction. Indigenous participants evaluated strange shiny objects through existing ideas of beauty, status and obligation.

Dominican settlements preserve ornaments in homes, refuse and burials. Following an object from manufacture through wear, repair, gifting and final deposit shows that adornment could build identity and memory. It also guards against calling every beautiful item elite treasure merely because museums prize it today.

A carved wooden duho from Hispaniola shows extraordinary woodworking and polished surface treatment. Its human-animal imagery and seat form connect leadership and ceremony, while its collection history and broad date demand caution. One museum object cannot define the beliefs or furniture of an entire archipelago.

sections.title: Homes, families, women and social life

items.text: Circular and oval post patterns reveal houses built with flexible organic materials. Caribbean examples differ from continental reconstructions and from colonial descriptions, so diameter, post spacing, rebuilding and storm exposure matter. A missing wall does not mean people lived outdoors; leaves, fiber and wood usually decay.

At El Flaco in the Dominican Republic, leveled house areas, surrounding mounds, ash, garbage, gardens and burials show domestic spaces repeatedly remade. Ancestors and daily work could share one landscape. Archaeologists read soil layers and postholes; they cannot simply copy a chronicler’s village sketch.

Jamaican house sizes and hillside terraces suggest some late communities used smaller residential groups, possibly nuclear-family households, while Puerto Rican sequences show different changes. Kinship remains debated because a roof group, work team, descent group and political community need not have identical membership.

Women appear in colonial stories filtered through European agendas, and objects cannot be assigned a gender automatically. Household archaeology at En Bas Saline instead compares activity areas, class and change after conquest. It finds persistence as well as disruption, warning against a single tale of instant social collapse.

Families cooked, repaired tools, cared for children, tended plants, fished, exchanged news and honored the dead, but tasks varied by household and life stage. Archaeology can locate hearths and work debris more securely than it can label “men’s work” or “women’s work” across 3,200 years.

sections.title: Children learned by living and doing

items.text: At Canímar Abajo, carbon and nitrogen isotopes from children and adult women support a local model: milk supplied most protein through about age two, plant supplements grew in importance, and weaning likely ended near three. This describes sampled Cuban burials, not a Caribbean-wide parenting rule.

Children probably learned swimming, paddling, fishing, plant knowledge, cooking, pottery and craft through observation, stories and practice. Finished objects prove expertise, while mistakes and small tools may hint at learners; no surviving timetable tells us lesson ages. Education was broader than a classroom.

Clothing rarely survives tropical soil, but cotton, fiber tools, ornaments and early accounts show bodies were dressed and decorated in varied ways. A bead or pendant could mark beauty, relationship, age or status. Researchers should not turn one contact-era description into everyone’s daily outfit.

Work and play can overlap. Swimming, racing, dancing, music, storytelling and ball games built skill and community, while formal plazas and carved boulders anchor some events archaeologically. We can identify a ball-court setting more confidently than the jokes, rules or cheers heard there.

A warm daily-life fact: people who grew up among islands likely learned the sea as a moving landscape, currents, cloud shapes, winds and familiar silhouettes mattered. Archaeology proves repeated voyaging and exchange, though it cannot recover each teaching rhyme. Skilled navigation was learned knowledge, not lucky drifting.

sections.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question

items.text: Bones and teeth can reveal injury, infection, anemia, diet and workload, but most illnesses leave no trace. Dental calculus adds oral microbes and food particles. Researchers describe patterns in specific cemeteries rather than diagnosing every community, and care by relatives often remains archaeologically invisible.

Vieques coprolites preserve parasite eggs and DNA consistent with exposure through fish, rodents, dogs and contaminated surroundings. That evidence documents real health burdens without proving people understood microbes. Parasites also connect diet, animal proximity, water and waste in ways a single artifact cannot.

Coprolite metagenomics can reconstruct gut microbes and foods even in a humid tropic, but Caribbean samples are rare and degraded. Differences between sampled Huecoid and Saladoid deposits are intriguing, not timeless biological traits. Laboratory controls matter because modern microbial contamination is everywhere, including on scientists.

No toilet type is securely attributable to this atlas umbrella. People could use peripheral places, pits, middens or fields, and tropical decay erases waste. Archaeologists need concentrated fecal chemistry, parasite eggs and convincing feature context before calling a hole a latrine rather than storage or rubbish.

Plants certainly served food and other needs, but identifying medicine requires context, residue or careful historical evidence. A Smithsonian guide to Guiana medicinal plants is useful later comparison for nearby living knowledge, not a prescription book for ancient islanders. Freshwater access likewise varied sharply by island.

Burials under or near household spaces, carved zemí figures, cave imagery, duhos and plazas show that ancestors, powerful beings and ceremony shaped some communities. Meanings changed across time and place. Similar-looking objects may participate in different stories, and descendant interpretations deserve space beside museum labels.

Petroglyphs and pictographs are meaningful images, not automatically writing. Around the Jacaná ball court, recording each boulder’s placement helps connect imagery with movement and ceremony. Without a demonstrated sign system tied to speech, no honest transliteration or sentence-level translation can be supplied.

Leadership ranged from household influence to powerful caciques, while alliances and obligations crossed islands. Rich objects and plazas can indicate rank, yet chroniclers filtered Indigenous politics through European categories. “Chiefdom” is a model to test locally, not a title for every society inside the polygon.

Spanish invasion brought organized violence, fort building, tribute demands and campaigns against resistance. Indigenous people fought, fled, negotiated, sabotaged and formed new alliances. Calling the outcome “contact” alone hides force; calling islanders passive victims hides their decisions and the colonizers’ incomplete control.

Raiding and enslavement reshaped coasts and islands. Colonial officials could label opponents “Caribs” to make capture appear legal, and enslavement continued through exceptions even after the New Laws. Those categories served power; they cannot be projected backward as clean ethnic borders on this map.

The atlas label supplies no language. Taíno and Lokono belong to Arawakan histories, while Kalinago language history, multilingualism and colonial naming are more complex. Shared words, pottery or ancestry cannot prove everyone spoke alike. “Arawakan” is a language-family relationship, not one timeless Caribbean nation.

Contemporaneous written-language sample: none can be responsibly attributed to this exact record. Indigenous Caribbean communities carried rich oral, musical and visual traditions, but no securely deciphered local script yields original text, transliteration and translation. Borrowing nearby Maya glyphs or later European spellings would fabricate an umbrella voice.

At LaSoye Point in Dominica, Cayo pottery beside European goods records early commerce in a place exposed by storm erosion. Indigenous people selected, reused and reinterpreted imports. Trade did not make the encounter equal: plantation settlement and war soon narrowed the choices available to island communities.

A Lucayan genome shares ancestry with present-day Puerto Rican people, and broader studies also find Indigenous biological continuity. Genetics is only one strand: survival also lives in family memory, food, craft, place names, activism and community belonging. No DNA percentage can certify or cancel an identity.

Kalinago people in Dominica maintain their territory, governance, farming, basketry, canoe knowledge and public cultural life. Taíno and other descendants likewise organize across the Caribbean and diaspora. The atlas ends this catchall in 1700 because its taxonomy changes; living communities make extinction language both false and harmful.

ending.text: At 1700 the exact atlas id disappears after shrinking to one small Amazon-mouth polygon. That endpoint does not match a single defeat, migration, language death or cultural extinction. Colonial states expanded through war, disease, slavery and displacement, while Indigenous people resisted, moved, formed new alliances and maintained families, knowledge and identities. Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and other descendant communities remain living peoples, so this card records editorial continuity rather than a fall and names no automatic successor.
